You are synthesizing technical specifications from 3 AI models for "Spares and Replacements" in the context of Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing.

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements (0B)
Accepted scope: Spares programme for robots, plant, tugs and power, including precision spares imported from Earth.

Round-2 proposals for this item (per model; not approved as numbers):
- add · spares / replacements · supported by all (Gemini as a 20% inventory buffer in missing items) · quantity: 1 programme · cost: Claude $0.5–1.5B; GPT $0.8–2.5B excl. robots · confidence: low

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts; bom-0-2 Mining Robots; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs; bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure; bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-10 Mission Operations; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply; bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve.

State quantities and costs as ranges with their basis, split 0A and 0B where the item spans both,
and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

## Model Specifications:

## Claude Opus 5.5

# bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements: Technical Proposal

**Item:** bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements (Phase 0B, with a small 0A enabling slice)
**Baseline context:** NEA-co-located Fe-Ni beneficiation and primary processing; MW-class EP tugs; SEL1 receiving node (D-04 interim); iodine reference propellant with argon alternate (D-05 interim); uncrewed.
**Author position:** opinionated engineering proposal. Every number is a planning range with its basis stated; none is an approved value.

---

## 1. Executive summary

1. **The spares programme is a logistics system, not a stockpile.** It covers four things:
   - the hardware (ORUs, wear parts, attrition replacements);
   - a three-echelon supply chain (Earth → SEL1 → NEA);
   - a robot-serviceable interface standard;
   - a reliability-data loop that sizes stock from failure physics.

   Flat percentage buffers, such as Gemini's 20%, are rejected.

2. **Make SEL1 the logistics hub and tug-servicing point.** The NEA site holds a forward depot sized to cover a 2.5–4 year resupply lead time.
   - Spares ride the outbound, near-empty tug leg in standard Logistics Pods.
   - The outbound leg has spare payload capacity, so spares cost almost nothing in tug Δv.
   - The cost that matters is Earth launch (bom-0-8) and hardware.

3. **Three drivers dominate.** They are, in order:
   - EP thruster wear-out on the tug fleet, which depends on the propellant choice.
   - Plant and robot wear at the regolith interface.
   - Robot attrition.

   Structure, arrays and avionics are second-order if they are designed with internal redundancy.

4. **0B cost over a 10-year production campaign is P10 $1.1B / P50 $2.0B / P90 $3.4B (FY2026), hardware plus logistics engineering, excluding launch.** That is about $200M/yr at steady state.
   - Mass imported from Earth is 150–600 t over the campaign (central ~270 t, ~27 t/yr).
   - This is roughly 15–30 kg imported per tonne of product delivered.
   - Launch of this mass is costed in bom-0-8 and is a further $0.3–1.8B.

5. **0A slice: $20–50M (central $30M).** It funds the ORU interface standard, the sparing model, the reliability database, and the test ORUs flown on the bom-0-12 pathfinder.

6. **Robotic ORU exchange at the NEA surface is a project-ending technology.** Under D-02 it must reach TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waiver before KDP-0B.

7. **Unit cost of sustainment is a gate-relevant number.** At P50, spares alone cost ~$150 per kg of product delivered. This should go to the economics gate as a headline. It does not break a capability programme (D-01), but it should end any claim that Phase 0 Fe-Ni is cheap.

---

## 2. Scope boundary (to avoid double-counting)

| Included in bom-0-14 | Excluded (owner) |

| ORUs, LRUs and wear parts for robots, plant, tugs and site power, from start of 0B operations | Initial fleets and day-one installed redundancy (bom-0-2, -3, -4, -5) |
| Whole-unit attrition replacements for robots after initial deployment | Initial robot fleet incl. day-one hot spares (bom-0-2) |
| Initial provisioning (IP) of NEA forward depot and SEL1 cache | SEL1 node structure and its own spares (bom-0-13); bom-0-14 specifies the cache interface |
| Logistics Pods (standard spares carriers) and their attach interface | Tug hardpoints themselves (bom-0-4) |
| Logistics engineering, sparing analytics, obsolescence management, lifetime buys of EEE parts | Life tests and qualification campaigns (bom-0-11) |
| Spares acceptance testing, packaging, ground depot | Launch and delivery to SEL1 (bom-0-8), for which bom-0-14 supplies the mass manifest |
| Block-upgrade ORUs (reliability growth delivered via the swap path) | Ops staffing and maintenance planning labour (bom-0-10) |
| Optional 0B Local Fabrication Cell for wear parts (gated option) | EP propellant (bom-0-16), comms ground segment (bom-0-9) |
| ORU end-of-life disposition hardware (retention and storage of failed units) | Debris policy and thresholds (bom-0-15), against which bom-0-14 complies |
| — | Unknown-unknown reserve above P50 (bom-0-17) |

**Rule:** spares follow the hardware they serve. Site-mounted comms terminals and tug transponders are spared here, because they are robot, plant, tug or power flight hardware. The ground segment is not.

**Upstream sizing assumptions** (owned by other items; replace them when those baselines freeze):

|---|---|---|---|
| Delivered product | 1.3 kt/yr | 0.6–2.5 | Re-assessment agreed band |
| 0B production campaign | 10 yr | 8–12 | My costing horizon |
| Mining/haul robots | 16 × 1.0 t | 10–30 × 0.5–1.5 t | Feed ~15–25 kt/yr at 8–15 wt% metal, 70% recovery |
| Processing plant dry mass | 60 t | 30–120 t | Parallel trains (2–4) |
| Site power | 1.0 MWe, 3 MWh | 0.5–2 MWe, 0.5–15 MWh | Agreed storage band |
| Tug fleet | 14 × 1.5 MWe | 10–18 × 1.0–2.5 MWe | Agreed band |
| Tug dry mass | 25 t | 15–45 t | ~180 W/kg arrays, ~5 kg/kW EP string |
| EP thruster | 100 kW-class Hall, 15 active + 3 redundant per 1.5 MWe tug | 50–200 kW units | Reference; argon may force a different thruster type |
| Tug thrust time | 5,000 h/yr | 3,500–7,000 | ~2 yr NEA–SEL1 round trips, coast phases |
| Installed 0B dry hardware | ~480 t | 230–1,100 t | Sum of the above |

---

## 3. Design philosophy

### 3.1 Eight principles

1. **Size spares from physics, not percentages.** Each ORU's stock comes from three inputs:
   - its demand process (random failure, wear-out, or attrition);
   - the resupply lead time at its echelon;
   - a stock-out risk target tied to its criticality.

   A flat 20% buffer is roughly right for nothing. Ground-engaging tools consume about 250% of their installed mass over 10 years, while primary structure needs 0%.

2. **Design for replacement rather than repair.**
   - At the NEA site, maintenance is Level 2: robots remove and replace ORUs.
   - There is no component-level repair in 0B except tether splicing and wear-part changes.
   - Component repair needs dexterity, contamination control and test equipment that cost more than the parts they save.

3. **Commonality is the strongest cost lever.** One actuator family, one battery module, one avionics computer, one 25 kW power-converter module, and one ORU interface family serve robots, plant, tugs and site power. The target is ≤400 ORU part numbers for the whole 0B system. Each unique part number carries roughly fixed costs: qualification, safety stock, and obsolescence tracking.

4. **Put the long lead times on the short legs.**
   - Tugs are serviced at SEL1, which is about 1 year from an Earth order.
   - The NEA site is 2.5–4 years from an Earth order and holds only what NEA hardware needs.
   - Class-L tug ORUs (thrusters, array segments) are not stocked at the NEA.

5. **Degrade gracefully.**
   - Plant runs in parallel trains.
   - Tugs carry N+k thruster and PPU redundancy sized to complete one round trip at ≥99% probability without service.
   - The robot fleet is sized for 80% availability.

   Spares restore margin. They are not the first line of defence.

6. **The spares path is the upgrade path.** Field failures drive redesigned ORUs that drop into the same interface. 10–15% of the hardware budget is reserved for block-upgrade ORUs, which is where reliability growth happens.

7. **Nothing is jettisoned.** Failed ORUs are kept for one of three fates:
   - cannibalisation;
   - return to SEL1 on product tugs (selected units only);
   - storage in a tethered or contained scrap pod (bom-0-15 compliance).

   Packaging must not shed: no loose MLI and no outgassing foams.

8. **Local manufacture is an option, not a baseline.** Fe-Ni wear parts made on site are attractive: wear parts are about 40% of spares mass but only about 10% of cost. However, the 0B baseline must close without local manufacture (§8.3).

### 3.2 What I am deliberately not proposing

- **No crewed or human-dexterity repair.** This follows from the uncrewed Phase 0 decision.
- **No return-to-Earth repair loop.** The return Δv and schedule kill it. Root-cause analysis relies on in-situ inspection imagery, plus a small number of units returned to SEL1 for inspection by node robotics.
- **No battery-heavy site architecture as a default.** If site power sits on a rotating NEA surface with a 3–8 h day, the battery cycles 1,000–3,000 times a year and becomes a consumable that dominates spares mass. I recommend that bom-0-5 strongly prefer a free-flying or polar-mast array that avoids eclipse (§5.4).

---

## 4. System architecture

### 4.1 Logistics network

```

 │  - robot ORU line            │ bom-  │    array segments, PPU modules)    │
 │  - EEE lifetime-buy store    │ 0-8   │  - NEA-bound pods staged           │
 │ Ground Depot & Acceptance    │══════>│ TUG SERVICING: node manipulator,   │
 │  - kitting into Logistics Pod│launch │  swap Class-L/M tug ORUs between   │
 │  - TVAC sample / functional  │       │  trips (24–72 h per tug visit)     │
 │ Sparing model + inventory DB │       │ Failed-unit inspection bay         │

                │ reorder (s,S) policy           │ outbound tug  │ inbound tug
                │ lead time 9–24 mo to SEL1      │ carries 1 Pod │ carries product
                │                                │ (5–10 t)      │ + selected
                ▼                                ▼ 6–18 mo       │ failed ORUs
       ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │ ECHELON E0: NEA FORWARD DEPOT                                     │
       │  Docked Pods (2–4 at any time) + shaded rack, 0–25 °C stores,     │
       │  heater power 2–6 kW                                              │
       │  Contents: robot ORUs, wear parts, tethers, plant ORUs, power     │

```

### 4.2 Why SEL1 is the hub

- **Every tug passes SEL1.** It is the product destination under D-04, so tug servicing there costs no extra trip.
- **Lead time.** Earth-to-SEL1 delivery is about a quarter of the Earth-to-NEA lead time. For random-failure ORUs, safety stock scales as about √(λ·L), so tug safety stock falls by roughly half when tugs are spared at SEL1 rather than at the NEA.
- **Fallback if D-04 flips.** If the 0B gate moves the receiving node (e.g., to SEL4/5 or cislunar), the hub moves with it. The architecture is location-agnostic as long as the hub sits on the product route.

### 4.3 Pod flow check

- **Demand:** ~27 t/yr central, 15–60 t/yr range.
- **Supply:** 6–9 outbound tug departures per year at 5–10 t pod each gives 30–90 t/yr capacity.
- **Margin:** at the high-demand end with a small fleet, the margin is thin. This makes a constraint on bom-0-4: **every tug must accept one Logistics Pod outbound without reducing its product capacity inbound.** The pod is dropped at the NEA before loading product.

---

## 5. Technical specifications

### 5.1 ORU interface standard (PD-ORU-1), delivered in 0A

| Class | Mass | Envelope (max) | Handler | Swap time target (incl. checkout) | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S | ≤25 kg | 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.6 m | Robot manipulator end-effector | ≤1 h | Sensors, avionics cards, cathodes, valves, cutter teeth cassettes |
| M | 25–500 kg | 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.5 m | Robot pair or plant gantry; SEL1 node arm | ≤8 h | Drive actuators, 25 kW PPU modules, pumps, battery modules (10 kWh), tether reels |
| L | 0.5–5 t | 2.5 × 2.5 × 4 m | SEL1 node arm, plant gantry, dedicated fixture | ≤72 h | 100 kW thrusters (incl. gimbal), array segments (25–50 kW), crusher assemblies, robot chassis |

**Mechanical interface**
- Self-aligning guide cone with a capture envelope of ±25 mm and ±3°.
- Single-actuator latch with preload ≥5 kN (S), ≥20 kN (M), ≥80 kN (L).
- Latch life ≥200 cycles.

**Electrical interface**
- *Low-voltage bus:* 120 V DC, ≤5 kW per connector. Dust-tolerant: shuttered, with wiper seals, scoop-proof, mate-under-dust tested.
- *HV path:* 1–3 kV for robot tether power and site PMAD, through a separate shuttered HV connector rated for ≥100 mate cycles in regolith-dust environment. This connector is the single highest-risk interface item.
- *Low-power Class-S ORUs (<200 W):* contactless inductive power and optical data, which removes exposed pins entirely.

**Data and thermal**
- *Data:* SpaceWire or TSN Ethernet, with an ORU electronic ID (EEPROM plus optical fiducial/2D code) read before latch closure.
- *Thermal:* conductive interfaces only at the NEA, with no fluid quick-disconnects in regolith dust. Fluid-loop plant components are spared as sealed assemblies including their own heat exchanger. Fluid QDs are allowed for tug ORUs at SEL1.

**Materials**
- No elastomeric seals on stored ORUs; use metal C-seals.
- Dry lubricants (MoS₂/WS₂ sputtered) or space-grade PFPE with a demonstrated 10-year shelf life.
- Iodine-compatible materials where ORUs see propellant (bom-0-16 / bom-0-4 coordination).

### 5.2 Logistics Pod

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Gross capacity | 10 t (5 t typical load) |
| Tare | 12–18% of gross (1.2–1.8 t) |
| Envelope | Fits a 9 m-class fairing; internal racks 2.4 × 2.4 × 5 m |
| Thermal | Passive MLI enclosure (non-shedding outer layer) plus 300–800 W heaters from host; stores 0 to +25 °C; batteries at 30–50% SOC, 0–15 °C |
| Radiation | ≥3 mm Al-equivalent around EEE ORU bays; 3-year transit dose budget |
| Interfaces | Tug hardpoint (bom-0-4), PD-ORU-1 Class-L latch at the depot, inventory telemetry via host (≤1 kbps) |
| Reuse | Pods stay at the NEA as depot storage and finally as a sealed scrap/retention vault; no return |
| Quantity | 25–45 over the campaign (central 35) |

### 5.3 Sparing method

**Demand classes**
- **R, random failure (exponential):** avionics, power electronics, sensors. Fleet demand rate λ = N·d/MTBF, where N is installed population and d is duty hours per year.
- **W, wear-out (deterministic plus scatter):** thrusters, cathodes, cutters, liners, crucibles, batteries. Demand is installed population × usage / life, with Weibull β = 2–4 scatter and 10–20% infant mortality.
- **A, attrition (catastrophic loss):** whole robots, tethers. Annual loss probability per unit p_A.

**Stock level per echelon:** smallest S such that P(demand over L > S) ≤ α, where:
- α = 2% for criticality-1 items (those whose loss stops production);
- α = 10% for criticality-2 items;
- α = 25% for criticality-3 items.

The full model is a multi-echelon METRIC-type optimisation coupled to a Monte Carlo tug-traffic simulation. The 0A deliverable optimises availability per dollar across all ORUs jointly, not item by item.

**Worked examples (central assumptions):**

| ORU | Echelon | Population | Demand basis | λ (fleet/yr) | Lead L | Mean demand over L | Stock (α) | Unit mass |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robot drive actuator | E0 NEA | 96 (16 × 6) | R/W, MTBF 20 kh, 4,380 h/yr | 21 | 3.0 yr | 63 | 77 (α=2%) | 8 kg |
| Robot tether (300 m, 2 kV) | E0 | 16 | A, 0.8/robot-yr | 13 | 3.0 yr | 38 | 49 (α=2%) | 60 kg |
| 25 kW PPU module | E1 SEL1 | 840 (14 × 60) | R, MTBF 500 kh, 8,760 h/yr | 15 | 1.0 yr | 15 | 23 (α=2%) | 50 kg |
| 100 kW Hall thruster | E1 SEL1 | 210 active | W, 30 kh life, 5,000 h/yr | 35 | 1.0 yr | 35 | 46 (α=2%, incl. infant) | 200 kg |
| Plant crusher liner set | E0 | 3 trains | W, ~6 kt feed per set | 3 | 3.0 yr | 9 | 12 (α=10%) | 400 kg |

The actuator example shows the leverage. Doubling MTBF to 40 kh roughly halves the NEA actuator stock and its 3-year pipeline mass. **A reliability dollar spent in bom-0-2 design returns several spares dollars here.** I recommend a formal trade, with joint authority between bom-0-2 and bom-0-14, before robot CDR.

### 5.4 Demand drivers by subsystem (central, 10-year campaign)

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Tug EP thrusters and cathode ORUs | 210 positions, 5,000 h/yr, life 30 kh; ~300 thrusters + ~400 cathodes | 62 | 450 | Propellant (iodine cathode erosion; argon may need a different thruster); life 15–60 kh |

| E | Robot attrition (whole units) | 10%/robot-yr × 16 robots × 10 yr = 16 units | 16 | 140 | p_A = 5–25%/yr is the least-known number in the item |
| F | Robot ORUs, tethers, batteries (10–50 kWh) | ~10%/yr of fleet mass; batteries 3 × fleet | 15 | 230 | Dust ingress, HV tether abrasion |
| G | Robot ground-engaging wear parts | ~20 kt/yr excavated × 50–200 g/t wear ÷ ~30% usable fraction | 40 | 70 | Local-manufacture candidate |

| J | Site power (array segments, battery modules, PMAD, radiators) | 3 MWh × 1.5 replacements central | 45 | 70 | Eclipse cycling: 5 t (free-flyer) to 190 t (15 MWh surface, 4 replacements) |
| — | Subtotal hardware | | 261 | 1,800 | |
| K | Logistics infrastructure (pods, cache fixtures, ground depot, GSE) | 35 pods + depot | (pod tare in mass below) | 90 | |
| L | Logistics engineering, analytics, obsolescence, acceptance | ~8% of hardware | — | 150 | |
| | **Total (deterministic central)** | | **~270 t incl. ~35 t pod tare and ~25 t residual safety stock, less double-counts** | **~2,040** | |

**Cost-per-mass basis used:**

| Category | Basis |
|---|---|
| Precision electronics and mechanisms | $20–40k/kg |
| Robots | $8–10k/kg |
| Thrusters in production quantity | ~$7.5k/kg (~$1.5M per 100 kW unit) |
| Arrays | $30–150/W (central $75/W ≈ $13k/kg) |
| Space-hardened Li-ion packs | $1.5–6/Wh |
| Qualified wear parts | $1.5–3k/kg |

These are recurring production costs. Spares NRE sits with the parent item in bom-0-11.

**Two consequential observations**
- **Cost and mass are concentrated in different places.** Tugs are about 46% of cost and about 30% of mass. Wear parts plus batteries are about 13% of cost and about 50% of mass.
  - Cost reduction comes from thruster life and commonality.
  - Mass (launch) reduction comes from wear-part local manufacture and from killing eclipse cycling.
- **Thruster life is the single largest swing.** At 15 kh life the A-line roughly doubles; at 60 kh it roughly halves to cathode-dominated.

  Magnetically shielded Hall thrusters have demonstrated pole/channel erosion lifetimes well beyond 30 kh on xenon. The open question is cathode and wall-material behaviour on iodine (reactive, corrosive) or argon (poor Hall efficiency at this scale). This is why D-05's life tests directly gate this budget.

## 6. Subsystems breakdown and interfaces

### 6.1 Programme work breakdown

```
bom-0-14 Spares & Replacements
├── 14.1 Logistics Engineering (0A+0B)
```

## 7. Autonomy, control and communications

**Maintenance Executive (ME), onboard the site controller**
- Runs prognostics and health management (PHM) on every ORU: current signatures, vibration, temperature, thruster discharge oscillation, battery impedance.
- Schedules pre-emptive swaps during low-production windows.
- Tracks inventory by serial number and maintains a digital twin of depot contents.

**Light time and supervision**
- NEA one-way light time is 2–20 min, depending on the target and epoch.
- Swaps therefore execute autonomously. Ground approves in a supervisory mode for criticality-1 swaps; routine Class-S/M swaps proceed without ground approval.
- Safe-mode rule: a failed swap leaves the ORU latched or parked, never free.

**Verification before install**
- The robot reads the ORU electronic ID and optical code.
- The ME confirms the part number, configuration revision and shelf-life status.
- A built-in test runs before the ORU is returned to service.
- Wrong-revision installs are blocked in software.

**Reorder logic**
- Lead-time-aware (s, S) policy, run on the ground in bom-0-10, using fleet telemetry.
- Reorders roll into the next available outbound pod. Monthly reconciliation runs against the digital twin.

**Data budget**
- Inventory and PHM summary: about 1–10 kbps average.
- Failure-event imagery and teardown video: 1–5 GB per event, with 10–40 events per year.
- This is well inside any credible bom-0-9 allocation and is not a driver.

**Cannibalisation policy**
- Allowed by rule, with a designated "donor" robot retired when fleet availability exceeds target.
- The ME must prevent a cannibalisation spiral: never strip more than one operating unit to restore another.

## 8. Manufacturing considerations

### 8.1 Earth production strategy

**Keep the thruster and PPU line warm.** About 30–50 thrusters per year is a genuine production rate. Spares and the initial tug build should share one line and one supplier qualification. A lifetime buy for thrusters is wrong, because the design will change with life data.

**Make a lifetime buy of rad-hard EEE parts at KDP-0B.**
- Scope: processors, FPGAs and HV power semiconductors, for 12–15 years of demand plus 30%.
- Cost: about $40–80M inside line L.
- Rationale: obsolescence of rad-hard parts on a 10-year horizon is close to certain.

**Batch acceptance for wear parts; full functional test for precision ORUs.**
- Thermal-vacuum testing applies to sample units per lot (1 in 5 to 1 in 10), not every unit.
- This is about 30% cheaper than per-unit TVAC and is justified by commonality and production volume.

**Shelf life**
- Spares spend up to 3 years in transit and depot.
- Qualification (bom-0-11) must include a 3-year storage-equivalent test for batteries, lubricants, adhesives and HV insulation.

### 8.2 Configuration control

All spares are built to the frozen baseline (§1 re-assessment directive). Block upgrades are issued as new part numbers with a documented form-fit-function interchange. Mixed-revision fleets are expected and tracked.

### 8.3 Optional 0B Local Fabrication Cell (LFC)

**What it would do:** produce simple wear parts from local Fe-Ni product, such as cutter bodies, bucket edges, liner backing plates and structural brackets.

**Material issues**
- Native kamacite (Fe with ~5–7% Ni) is soft, about 150–200 HV, and makes poor wear parts unalloyed.
- Troilite (FeS) inclusions risk sulfur embrittlement.

**Candidate routes**
- Sinter or cast Fe-Ni bodies with hardfacing from imported WC-Co powder. The import is about 5–10% of part mass.
- Alloy with an imported C/Cr/Mo masterbatch.

**Value and cost**
- Potential saving: 40–80% of G+I mass (35–70 t over 10 years), or about $50–250M of avoided launch at bom-0-8 rates.
- Hardware saving is small, about $50–100M.
- LFC cost: $60–150M including qualification.

**Recommendation:** carry the LFC as a gated option decided around 0B year 3, using in-situ wear data. Do not carry it in the baseline. It is TRL 2–3 today.

## 12. Open engineering questions

1. **Thruster wear on the selected propellant.** What are the cathode and wall-erosion lifetimes of a 100 kW-class thruster on iodine, and on argon? Does argon force a different thruster class (RF gridded, or other), with different ORU sizes? This is the largest single budget lever.

2. **Robot attrition physics.** What is the realistic annual loss rate for tethered robots working ordinary-chondrite regolith in milli-g? The pathfinder must log at least about 200 robot-hours of fault data to bound it.

3. **Eclipse cycling.** Will the bom-0-5 site power avoid eclipse? This alone moves spares mass by up to about 150 t.

4. **Wear rates.** What are the ground-engaging-tool and liner wear rates (g/t) in regolith and boulder simulant under vacuum? Terrestrial values of 10–200 g/t may not transfer because of vacuum cold-welding and the absence of lubricating films.

5. **Tug repair location.** Should tugs be serviced only at SEL1? Or should NEA site robots carry Class-M tug spares for contingencies, accepting duplicate inventory? Current view: a minimal Class-S/M tug contingency kit only at the NEA (~2 t).

6. **N+k thruster redundancy versus spares.** What thruster and PPU redundancy per tug minimises the combined cost of tug mass and spares, while meeting ≥99% completion of a round trip without service? A joint trade with bom-0-4 is needed.

7. **Local manufacture.** Is Fe-Ni with imported hardfacing durable enough to replace Earth wear parts? What import fraction makes the LFC break even against bom-0-8 launch prices?

8. **Ownership boundary at SEL1.** Does the SEL1 node manipulator (bom-0-13) carry the Class-L servicing role, or does bom-0-14 need its own servicing free-flyer? Current view: node manipulator, specified by bom-0-14.

9. **Failed-unit return.** How many failed units should return to SEL1 for root-cause analysis, and is in-situ imaging enough for the top-20 failure modes?

10. **Licensing and retention.** What retention requirement will the licensing state impose on failed ORUs, under D-03 ALARP? Will scrap need eventual disposal rather than indefinite retention?

11. **If D-04 flips.** If the 0B gate moves the receiving node away from SEL1, does the hub move with it? How much of the SEL1 cache investment (fixtures, ~$20–40M) is stranded?

## 1. Recommended Approach and Design Philosophy
For a fully uncrewed, high-throughput (1 kt/yr) industrial operation at a Near-Earth Asteroid (NEA), maintenance cannot rely on ad-hoc repairs. My design philosophy for the Phase 0 Spares and Replacements program is based on **Orbital Replacement Units (ORUs)** and **Predictive Logistics**. 

Instead of repairing components, autonomous maintenance robots will swap standardized ORUs. We categorize spares into two tiers:
1.  **Consumables & High-Wear Items**: Crusher jaws, EP (Electric Propulsion) thruster grids, cutting heads, and tether segments. These have predictable degradation curves.
2.  **Random-Failure Items**: Avionics, power management and distribution (PMAD) modules, and sensors. These require a statistical buffer.

**Disagreement with Round-2 Figures:** I reject GPT's upper bound of $2.5B (excluding robots) as excessively pessimistic for a 1 kt/yr operation. If spares cost $2.5B, the baseline hardware reliability is fundamentally unsuited for space mining. I align closer to Claude's $0.5–$1.5B range, specifically targeting **$0.6B–$1.4B**, assuming a 20-25% mass buffer for wear items and a 10% buffer for avionics.

## 2. System Architecture

The spares architecture relies on a primary depot at the NEA and a secondary staging node at SEL1. MW-class cargo tugs will transport precision spares from Earth (via SEL1) to the NEA on their return trips (which are otherwise flying empty or carrying only EP propellant).

```text
[Earth Manufacturing]
       | (Launch)
       v
[SEL1 Receiving Node] ---> (Spares Cache & Tug Integration)
       |
       | (MW-Class Cargo Tugs - Return Trip)
       v
[NEA Processing Site] ---> [Automated Spares Depot]
                               |--> Mining Robots (Tool swaps)
                               |--> Processing Plant (Crucible/Crusher ORUs)
                               |--> Site Power (Inverter/Array ORUs)
```

## 3. Technical Specifications and Sizing
*   **Total Spares Mass Allocation (0B):** ~15–20% of the initial deployed mass (approx. 40–60 tonnes of spares for a ~250–300 tonne initial NEA deployment).
*   **High-Wear Buffer:** 30% of active unit count (e.g., if 10 mining robots are active, 3 full sets of replacement tracks/tools are stocked).
*   **Avionics/Random Failure Buffer:** 10% of active unit count, utilizing N-modular redundancy for critical paths.
*   **Storage Environment:** Passive thermal control (radiators/MLI) keeping electronic spares between -20°C and +40°C. Mechanical spares stored exposed to vacuum.

## 4. Subsystems Breakdown and Interfaces
*   **Standardized Grapple Fixtures:** All ORUs must feature a unified electro-mechanical interface (e.g., an evolution of the ISS iLIDS or Androgynous Peripheral Attach System, scaled down for robotics) allowing a single type of maintenance manipulator to swap any part.
*   **Smart Spares RFID/NFC:** Every spare includes a passive RFID tag and a low-power health-monitoring circuit to verify it survived launch and transit before installation.
*   **Automated Spares Depot (ASD):** A localized rack system at the NEA processing plant. Includes a dust-mitigated "clean zone" for sensitive sensor ORUs, utilizing electrostatic dust shields (EDS).

## 5. Autonomy, Control, and Communication
*   **Predictive Maintenance (PdM):** The ground segment (bom-0-9) will run digital twins of all NEA assets. Telemetry (vibration, thermal gradients, current draw) will predict failures before they occur.
*   **Autonomous Swapping:** The actual physical swap of an ORU will be executed autonomously by site maintenance robots, supervised by Earth via delayed telemetry. 
*   **Safe-Mode Integration:** If an ORU fails during a swap, the system must autonomously revert to a safe state (e.g., locking the mechanism) to await Earth intervention.

## 6. Development Roadmap and Technology Readiness
*   **Phase 0A (Pathfinders):** Focus on validating the ORU electro-mechanical interface in dusty, microgravity environments (TRL 4 to 6). Test autonomous robotic swapping on the 0A demonstrator.

| Spare procurement and supplier-held inventory | Programme-wide organization: bom-0-7 |
| Hardware repair/refurbishment contracts | Routine ground control and operational staffing: bom-0-10 |
| Packaging and preservation before shipment | Launch and transportation services: bom-0-8 |
| Spare thrusters and feed hardware | EP propellant purchases: bom-0-16 |
| Ordinary expected failures and planned wear-out replacements | Programme contingency and exceptional-loss reserve: bom-0-17 |

**Accounting rule:** Each serialized article has one procurement owner. An installed standby converter belongs to the original asset. An identical converter held in inventory belongs to bom-0-14.

---

## 2. Recommended design philosophy

### 2.1 Design for restoration, not merely survival

Traditional spacecraft redundancy keeps an asset functioning after a limited number of failures. An industrial system must also restore its configuration repeatedly.

I recommend three maintenance levels:

1. **Autonomous recovery:** isolate faults, reset electronics, reroute power, release overloads, and switch redundant strings.
2. **Robotic module replacement:** exchange sealed line-replaceable units, or LRUs.
3. **Controlled refurbishment:** repair selected returned modules in an enclosed work volume or on Earth.

Open-board electronic repair, precision bearing replacement, and internal thruster reconstruction should not be required for production continuity.

### 2.2 Standardize interfaces more aggressively than internal designs

A shared electrical connector is useful; a shared hidden defect across every tug is dangerous.

Standardize:

- Mechanical mounting and capture features.
- Power and data interfaces.
- Diagnostic records.
- Handling fixtures.
- Thermal connection classes.
- Replacement procedures.

Do not require one design for every critical component. Preserve qualified alternatives where common-cause failure would strand the fleet.

### 2.3 Make precision Earth imports explicit

Phase 0 should assume Earth supply for:

- Bearings, gearsets, and precision actuators.
- Radiation-tolerant electronics and sensors.
- High-voltage switches and insulation assemblies.
- Battery cells and battery-management electronics.
- Thrusters, cathodes, and precision feed components.
- Vacuum seals and specialized polymers.
- Solar cells and precision optical elements.

Local Fe–Ni manufacturing may eventually replace brackets, guards, ballast, simple fixtures, and some tooling. No reduction in critical spare holdings should be credited until the local process and resulting parts are qualified.

---

## 3. System architecture

```text
                 EARTH SUPPLIERS / REFURBISHMENT
                    |                    ^
        qualified spare hardware        | selected failed units
                    v                    |
             EARTH INVENTORY POOL
       screening / preservation / tracking
                    |
        launch and delivery: bom-0-8
                    |
        +-----------+-----------------------+
        |                                   |
        v                                   v
 TARGET-NEA SPARES STORE             RECEIVING-NODE STORE
 cold + conditioned inventory       SEL1 reference case
        |                           receiver-side spares;
        |                           optional consolidation
        v
 ROBOTIC EXCHANGE / REPAIR AREA
        |
        +--> mining and handling robots
        +--> beneficiation / Fe–Ni plant
        +--> site power and thermal systems
        +--> tugs when accessible for servicing

 EACH TUG:
 installed fault tolerance + small carried recovery kit
 + diagnostic records + safe-mode capability
```

The primary inventory location must follow the likely failure location.

- A critical plant drive stored at SEL1 does not protect asteroid production.
- A spare thruster at the asteroid cannot rescue an inaccessible tug midway through transfer.
- Earth inventory offers manufacturing flexibility, not prompt recovery.

### 3.1 Inventory tiers

| Tier | Location | Typical contents | Planning basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | Installed on operating asset | Redundant electronics, isolated power strings | Owned by original asset BOM |
| T1 | Carried on mobile asset | Small recovery modules, connectors, control electronics | Mass-limited; only physically exchangeable items |
| T2 | Asteroid site | Critical plant, robot, power, and serviceable tug modules | Initially 18–30 months of lead-time demand |
| T3 | Receiving node | Receiver spares and selected logistics stock | Route-dependent; not a substitute for T2 |
| T4 | Earth | Long-lead assemblies, supplier stock, refurbishment pool | Rolling forecast and production capability |

**Important limitation:** A tug-carried spare is only useful if the tug has a demonstrated means to install it. Otherwise, redundant installed strings—not loose spares—provide the in-transit recovery function.

---

## 4. Technical specifications

The values below are **proposed interface envelopes**, not claimed flight-qualified designs.

### 4.1 Replaceable-unit classes

| Class | Typical application | Mass | Approximate envelope | Handling method |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| S | Sensors, controllers, small valves | 2–25 kg | Up to 0.4 × 0.3 × 0.3 m | Single manipulator |
| M | Drives, converters, battery modules | 25–150 kg | Up to 1.0 × 0.7 × 0.6 m | Captured robotic exchange |
| L | Thruster strings, pump skids, furnace cartridges | 150–1,000 kg | Up to 2.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 m | Two-point capture and guided translation |
| XL | Array wings, radiator sections, whole robots | 1–5 t | Asset-specific, usually folded | Anchored handling fixture or servicing vehicle |

In microgravity, low weight does not mean easy handling. Replacement motions must be sized for inertia, reaction loads, flexible-body dynamics, and anchorage limitations.

### 4.2 Mechanical interface requirements

Recommended starting requirements:

- At least two independent capture features on modules above 25 kg.
- Captive fasteners and captive connector covers.
- No loose washers, cut wire, or discarded locking devices.
- Visible and machine-readable identity markings.
- Alignment features that engage before power or fluid connections.
- Coarse robotic approach tolerance of approximately ±10 mm and ±3°, followed by guided seating.
- Final alignment determined by the connector or coupling design; precision optical modules use a separate kinematic interface.
- Torque and seating-force verification during installation.
- Tool access from the planned service direction, verified with representative manipulators and protective enclosures.

Modules must be removable without disconnecting unrelated healthy systems wherever practical.

### 4.3 Electrical and data interfaces

- **Primary site distribution:** 1–3 kV DC reference architecture.
- **Service control power:** standardized isolated 28 V and/or 48 V rails.
- **Power exchange:** de-energized module replacement; no routine live mating of exposed high-voltage connectors.
- **Data:** redundant deterministic Ethernet or equivalent qualified network, with a low-rate independent safe-mode interface.
- **Identification:** serial number, hardware revision, firmware compatibility, operating limits, life history, and acceptance status.
- **Isolation:** positive verification of electrical discharge before tool access.
- **Compatibility:** connector keying must prevent iodine/argon, voltage-class, and incompatible firmware substitutions.

### 4.4 Thermal and fluid interfaces

Use separate interface families for:

1. Dry electronics with conductive thermal mounts.
2. Liquid-cooled power modules.
3. High-temperature process assemblies.
4. Propellant-exposed hardware.

Recommended features include:

- Double isolation where opening a loop could disable the plant.
- Leak checking before reconnecting a replacement section.
- Captured residual fluid and contamination monitoring.
- Segmentable radiator circuits.
- Standard radiator mechanical mounts where temperatures and coolant chemistry permit.

A universal coolant connection across the plant, batteries, and tug propulsion is **not** recommended.

### 4.5 Storage and preservation

| Storage mode | Contents | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| Passive protected storage | Structural parts, compatible dry mechanical assemblies | Dust exclusion, thermal cycling qualification, positive restraint |
| Conditioned electronics storage | Avionics, sensors, selected seals and polymers | Controlled temperature, radiation protection where justified |
| Battery storage | Battery replacement modules | Supplier-defined temperature and state of charge; periodic health checks |
| Propulsion-component storage | Thrusters, feed modules, sensitive materials | Chemistry-specific cleanliness and isolation |
| Clean process storage | Instrumentation and contamination-sensitive components | Sealed containers with witness samples |

Preliminary allowance:

- **Storage and exchange equipment delivered mass:** 5–12 t.
- **Conditioning and monitoring power:** approximately 5–20 kW average, strongly dependent on local thermal conditions.
- **Maintenance peak electrical load:** approximately 20–60 kW, excluding large process equipment already owned by the plant.

These loads must enter bom-0-5 power and thermal sizing; they are not free auxiliary capacity.

---

## 5. Initial quantities and replacement holdings

The following quantities describe a **provisional initial inventory and five-year procurement envelope**. They are not all delivered at once.

### 5.1 Mining and handling robots

For a 24-unit active fleet:

- **2–4 complete spare robots**, preferably fully commissioned before storage.
- Replacement actuator/drive modules equal to approximately **15–30% of installed positions initially**, then replenished from observed wear.
- **2–3 years of forecast abrasive wear parts** at the asteroid.
- Battery replacement capacity equal to **20–40% of installed robot battery energy initially**.
- Spare tether sections, reels, abrasion guards, end effectors, cameras, and high-voltage connector assemblies.

For 10–50 kWh onboard batteries, 24 robots contain approximately 0.24–1.2 MWh of battery capacity. The initial robot battery spare provision is therefore approximately **0.05–0.48 MWh**, depending on the selected fleet.

**Design preference:** Exchange contaminated end effectors as cartridges. Do not make manipulator joints carry uncontained abrasive processing loads.

### 5.2 Processing plant

For three partly independent trains:

- One replacement for each critical unique drive, feed mechanism, or control function that lacks an operational bypass.
- **1–2 complete replacement furnace or hot-zone cartridges**, if selected metallurgy uses this architecture.
- **2–4 replacement feed/beneficiation modules**, adjusted to actual train commonality.
- Multiple campaigns of liners, screens, cutters, seals, and dust-handling elements.
- Spare temperature, composition, mass-flow, and product-quality instrumentation.

Wear-part mass cannot yet be credibly fixed without representative material tests. The first industrial procurement should be gated by measured **wear per tonne processed**, including beneficiation rejects—not merely product output.

### 5.3 Cargo tugs

For the 12-tug sizing case:

- Replaceable thruster/cathode assemblies corresponding initially to approximately **10–20% of fleet-installed strings**.
- Power-processing and control spares corresponding to approximately **8–15% of installed replaceable units**.
- Spare attitude-control hardware, sensors, reaction-control valves where applicable, and communications electronics.
- **One complete uncommitted replacement tug option**, priced and contractually available, but not automatically purchased under this line.

Installed string counts must be derived from qualified thruster life. A 1.5 MWe tug may contain several independently isolated propulsion strings; “one spare thruster per tug” is not an adequate specification.

Whole-tug attrition is not automatically covered by an LRU inventory. The gate review must explicitly choose between:

- Operational fleet margin in bom-0-4.
- A funded whole-tug replacement under bom-0-14.
- Reduced contractual delivery after a loss.

### 5.4 Power and thermal systems

Across site and tug assets:

- Approximately **1.5–2.5 MWe of replacement array nameplate capacity at 1 AU**, initially divided between delivered and Earth-held stock.
- **10–20% of installed converter and switching modules**, differentiated by criticality.
- Approximately **0.2–0.6 MWh of site battery replacements**, in addition to robot battery stock.
- **5–10% of replaceable radiator area**, concentrated on standardized sections, isolation valves, and vulnerable interfaces.
- Spare deployment drives, harness sections, sensors, and power-distribution connectors.

Replacement arrays should be purchased in compatible blocks rather than as unique full spacecraft wings wherever the original asset design permits.

The array quantity is a planning allowance for damage, failed deployment, and replacement—not an assertion that ordinary degradation requires wholesale panel replacement within five years.

### 5.5 Mass estimate

| Hardware family | Five-year procurement mass |
|---|---:|
| Robot replacements and robot spares | 10–22 t |
| Plant replacement equipment and wear parts | 25–55 t |
| Tug propulsion and bus spares, excluding arrays | 10–24 t |
| Power, storage, and thermal replacement hardware | 18–45 t |
| Shared avionics, sensors, and communications modules | 2–5 t |
| Inventory fixtures, preservation, and exchange tools | 5–12 t |
| **Unpackaged total** | **70–163 t** |
| **Planning delivered mass including packaging allowance** | **80–180 t** |

Not all hardware must leave Earth. Approximately **45–60% of the five-year hardware mass** is a reasonable initial deployment planning allowance; the remainder is held, procured, or replenished later.

These are logistics inputs to bom-0-8, not launch costs included here.

---

## 6. Reliability and inventory sizing

### 6.1 Availability objectives

I recommend the following initial programme requirements:

- **Site productive availability:** 85–92%, excluding planned external power or communications constraints.
- **Delivery-system availability:** demonstrate sufficient fleet capacity to meet the signed delivery schedule with scheduled maintenance and ordinary failures.
- **Spare stockout contribution:** less than 1–2 percentage points of annual production unavailability.
- **Criticality-A item stockout probability:** target below 0.5–1% per replenishment interval.

These are proposed allocation targets. They require a system model; multiplying optimistic subsystem availability figures is not sufficient.

### 6.2 Inventory calculation

For an initial screening calculation:

\[
\lambda_i = N_i h_i T_L / MTBF_i
\]

where:

- \(N_i\) is the number of operating units.
- \(h_i\) is operating hours per year.
- \(T_L\) is effective replenishment lead time in years.
- \(MTBF_i\) is operating-hour mean time between failures.

Example:

- 12 operating units.
- 4,000 operating hours per year each.
- 1.25-year replenishment interval.
- 30,000-hour MTBF.

Expected demand is two units. Under an independent Poisson model, six spares provide approximately a **99.55% probability that demand does not exceed stock** during that interval.

That is a useful screening result, not a complete reliability claim. The final model must include:

- Wear-out rather than constant failure rates.
- Common-cause defects.
- Dust and thermal exposure correlation.
- Maintenance-induced failures.
- Failed replacement attempts.
- Shipment loss and missed launch opportunities.
- Manufacturing lead time and obsolescence.
- Cannibalization and repair yield.

### 6.3 Maintenance-time targets

Initial demonstrator targets:

| Operation | Target elapsed time under suitable access conditions |
|---|---:|
| Small electronics LRU exchange | 2–6 hours |
| Robot drive or battery exchange | 4–12 hours |
| Process cartridge replacement | 12–48 hours |
| Tug propulsion-string replacement at service location | 24–72 hours |
| Large array/radiator replacement | 2–7 days |

These include isolation, handling, installation, and checkout—not interplanetary transport.

---

## 7. Autonomy, control, and communications

### 7.1 Required autonomy

The maintenance system must independently:

1. Detect and classify faults.
2. Enter a stable isolated state.
3. Preserve diagnostic evidence.
4. Identify compatible available replacements.
5. Check whether the operation is authorized.
6. Execute verified exchange steps.
7. Stop safely on unexpected force, leakage, arcing, or geometry.
8. Perform post-installation tests.

Destructive disassembly, opening a major fluid loop, and changes to plant safety logic require ground authorization unless specifically pre-authorized for immediate hazard control.

### 7.2 Control architecture

Use:

- Deterministic safety interlocks.
- Model-based fault detection.
- Bounded robotic task execution.
- Vision and force/torque sensing.
- Independent verification of isolation and connector seating.

Learning-based perception may support inspection and localization. It should not be the sole authority for high-voltage isolation, containment opening, or irreversible tool actions.

### 7.3 Communications and records

Do not assume continuous low-latency Earth control.

Planning allocation for maintenance traffic:

- Approximately **0.1–2 GB/day averaged across routine activity**, depending on inspection policy.
- Event-driven diagnostic packages of approximately **1–20 GB**.
- Store-and-forward handling for high-resolution imagery.
- Low-rate fault summaries prioritized over bulk video.

The final allocation belongs in bom-0-9. These volumes are engineering assumptions, not a network commitment.

Every installed and stored module requires a persistent “digital traveler” containing acceptance data, exposure history, operating hours, repairs, firmware, and remaining-life estimate.

---

## 8. Manufacturing and supply-chain approach

### 8.1 Procurement strategy

- Qualify at least two sources for selected high-consequence electronics and mechanical interfaces where economically justified.
- Reserve manufacturing capacity for long-lead parts rather than buying all five-year inventory immediately.
- Make lifetime buys only where obsolescence risk exceeds storage and capital penalties.
- Procure initial and spare units from more than one accepted lot for common-cause risk control.
- Require supplier change notification and configuration traceability.

A low-price substitute that fits mechanically but has different firmware, outgassing, insulation, or propellant compatibility is not interchangeable.

### 8.2 Acceptance and storage testing

Each flight spare should receive:

- Electrical functional and insulation tests.
- Appropriate vacuum and thermal acceptance exposure.
- Leak tests where relevant.
- Connector mating verification.
- Software/firmware compatibility checks.
- Cleanliness verification.
- Baseline diagnostic signature capture.

Storage plans must include battery inspections, seal shelf-life tracking, and periodic functional checks. “Unused” is not synonymous with “flight-ready.”

### 8.3 Local manufacture

Permit local production first for noncritical items with straightforward inspection:

- Guards and covers.
- Tool adapters.
- Simple brackets.
- Handling fixtures.
- Temporary mechanical restraints.

Do not credit local metal production as a solution to precision-spares dependence during 0B.

---

## 9. Development roadmap and readiness

### 9.1 Phase 0A work

Although bom-0-14 is primarily a 0B procurement item, its architecture must be proven during 0A.

| 0A activity | Indicative cost | Accounting owner |
|---|---:|---|
| Reliability model, criticality ranking, interface definition | $4–8M | bom-0-11, with organization support |
| Exchange interfaces, tools, and ground demonstrations | $8–18M | bom-0-11 |
| Integrated pathfinder maintenance demonstration | $8–19M incremental allocation | bom-0-12 |
| **Total associated 0A effort** | **$20–45M** | **Not added again to bom-0-14** |

These are cross-programme planning allocations, not additional independent budget lines.

### 9.2 Readiness position

Many component technologies have substantial terrestrial or spacecraft heritage. That does **not** establish readiness of autonomous industrial maintenance at an asteroid.

The least mature combinations are likely to be:

- Dust-exposed robotic high-voltage module exchange.
- Anchored handling of large flexible modules.
- Repeated maintenance of microgravity beneficiation and metallurgy equipment.
- Long-storage activation after deep-space environmental exposure.
- Autonomous restoration after partially completed or failed exchanges.

Their actual TRL must be established by evidence, not assigned from component heritage.

### 9.3 Gates

**Internal 0A milestones: TRL 4–5**

- Representative dusty-vacuum connector trials.
- Repeated robotic exchange tests.
- Storage and activation trials.
- Demonstrated recovery from jammed or incorrectly seated modules.
- Initial reliability and inventory simulation.

**KDP-0B: TRL 6 in a relevant environment, without waivers for project-ending technologies**

Required evidence should include:

- Integrated exchange and recommissioning of critical modules.
- Representative contamination, thermal, electrical, and mechanical conditions.
- Demonstrated failure recovery—not only successful nominal replacement.
- A supportable inventory and resupply plan for the selected target.
- No unproven maintenance function whose failure ends the project.

If a critical exchange operation cannot reach the required readiness, redesign the asset for demonstrated lifetime or installed redundancy before committing to production.

---

## 10. Cost estimate

### 10.1 Conditional five-year 0B procurement

Constant 2026 dollars; ordinary expected replacements included.

| Cost element | Range |
|---|---:|
| Robot replacement hardware and wear spares | $80–180M |
| Plant replacement modules and process wear parts | $110–240M |
| Tug propulsion and bus replacement hardware, excluding arrays | $180–420M |
| Replacement power, batteries, and thermal hardware | $120–280M |
| Shared avionics, sensors, and communications spares | $50–120M |
| Storage equipment, preservation, fixtures, and exchange tooling | $40–100M |
| Spare acceptance, refurbishment contracts, configuration verification, and supplier inventory services | $70–210M |
| **Total bom-0-14** | **$650–1,550M** |

The endpoints are planning envelopes, not statistically derived confidence bounds.

### 10.2 Basis and sensitivities

Major drivers are:

1. **EP lifetime and replacement frequency.**
2. **Actual abrasive wear per tonne processed.**
3. **How much fleet electrical hardware is replaceable.**
4. **Target-specific replenishment time.**
5. **Required delivery assurance.**
6. **Commonality achieved without common-cause vulnerability.**

Array hardware should use the reassessment’s **$30–150/W hardware range**, with launch separate. For example, 1.5–2.5 MW of replacement array hardware alone spans approximately **$45–375M** if quantity and unit-price extremes are combined.

Consequently, the $120–280M power-and-thermal row assumes a narrower compatible procurement case within those broad extremes. If high array quantity and high unit pricing occur together, that row—and the programme estimate—must increase. They cannot be hidden inside contingency.

### 10.3 Procurement phasing

A reasonable starting profile is:

- **Initial inventory and enabling hardware:** roughly 45–60% of total hardware commitment.
- **Rolling replenishment and refurbishment:** roughly 40–55%, released against operating evidence.

These percentages describe procurement timing, not a requirement to launch the same fraction of total cost.

### 10.4 Position relative to round-2 proposals

**Claude: $0.5–1.5B.**  
Broadly consistent with the upper and central portions of this proposal. I would not adopt $0.5B as the protected baseline before wear and EP life are demonstrated. It leaves little room for robot replacements, fleet-wide power spares, or a long resupply interval.

**GPT: $0.8–2.5B excluding robots.**  
A defensible high-risk envelope, but too high as the default procurement case if it implicitly includes duplicate tugs, launch, qualification, or contingency. Its upper end may become appropriate with poor thruster life, high wear, expensive arrays, or purchases of whole replacement spacecraft.

**Gemini: 20% inventory buffer.**  
Reject as the primary sizing rule. Twenty percent may be excessive for durable structure and inadequate for a unique high-wear component. Inventory must be item-specific and lead-time-dependent.

---

## 11. Principal risks and mitigations

| Risk | Consequence | Recommended mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Common-cause component defect | Fleet-wide grounding despite large inventory | Lot diversity, selected alternate designs, rapid requalification path |
| Dust-damaged connectors | Repeated failed replacements | Protected interfaces, clean mating volumes, representative cycle tests |
| Underestimated abrasive wear | Frequent plant shutdown | 0A wear testing, cartridge design, large early wear-part holdings |
| Failed autonomous exchange | Healthy spare cannot restore service | Recovery fixtures, reversible procedures, demonstrated fallback states |
| Long resupply delay | Extended production loss | Site stock sized to actual delivery opportunities |
| Battery degradation in storage | Spare unavailable when needed | Controlled storage and periodic health checks |
| Tug failure away from service location | Spare inaccessible | Installed fault tolerance and trajectory-level rescue analysis |
| Spare becomes obsolete or incompatible | Inventory loses value | Configuration control and interface compatibility testing |
| Local repair creates contamination | Product rejection or hazardous debris | Enclosed repair operations and captured waste |
| Budget reduction removes “unused” stock | Reliability silently degrades | Tie inventory changes to contractual delivery-risk analysis |

### Contamination and debris

All replacement activity should satisfy ALARP and the interim programme ceiling once established through modelling, tests, and the licensing state.

For design development, require:

- Captive hardware.
- Captured cuttings and worn parts.
- Enclosed abrasive cleaning.
- No intentional release of failed modules.
- Positive inventory reconciliation after maintenance.
- Verified isolation before opening contaminated equipment.

A single mass-retention percentage is not sufficient: escaped particle size, velocity, chemistry, and trajectory matter. Detailed quantitative thresholds and compliance infrastructure remain under bom-0-15.

---

## 12. Open engineering questions before KDP-0B

1. **What are the actual replenishment opportunities for the selected asteroid?**  
   This may dominate inventory more than nominal component reliability.

2. **Which plant components exhibit wear proportional to feed mass rather than operating hours?**

3. **What thruster, cathode, and feed-system life is demonstrated at the selected operating point and propellant?**

4. **Can tugs reliably present propulsion modules for robotic replacement?**

5. **How much processing capacity remains after one train or a shared utility fails?**

6. **Which replacement modules genuinely benefit from commonality across plant, robot, and tug assets?**

7. **What fraction of radiator and array damage is repairable by module exchange?**

8. **Which stored components require conditioning power, and what happens after prolonged power loss?**

9. **What product-quality requalification is required after plant maintenance?**

10. **How much delivery shortfall can Phase 1 tolerate, and when should Earth-supplied material be activated as fallback?**

11. **Does the economics gate still close when realistic wear, replacement hardware, delivery, and operating costs are included?**

12. **Which maintenance functions are project-ending technologies under D-02?**

---

## 13. Final recommendation

Approve the **0A reliability, interface, and maintenance-demonstration work**, funded through the existing NRE and pathfinder lines. Do not authorize bulk 0B spares procurement yet.

At KDP-0B, require:

- A configuration-controlled parts and maintenance architecture.
- Demonstrated robotic replacement of critical modules.
- Target-specific lead-time and inventory modelling.
- Qualified EP and process-life evidence.
- An explicit whole-tug-loss policy.
- A five-year replacement budget linked to signed Phase 1 demand.
- A fallback plan using Earth-supplied material if production availability or metallurgy does not meet the contract.

**My preferred 0B baseline is a $0.65–1.55B modular spares programme, with approximately 80–180 t of five-year replacement hardware and packaging, delivered progressively.** Its purpose is not to make every asset immortal. It is to make ordinary failures recoverable without crew, without an emergency redesign, and without turning a single missing precision component into the end of Phase 0.

- **Replace, don't repair, at the NEA.** All three models adopt a modular replaceable-unit scheme, called ORUs by Claude and Gemini and LRUs by GPT. Site robots swap units autonomously.

Identity is an EEPROM plus optical code (Claude) or RFID/NFC (Gemini), and is checked before installation. Wrong-revision or incompatible installs are blocked.
- **The NEA site holds the primary forward stock.**
  - Only stock at the NEA protects production, so NEA-critical spares are held there.
  - Earth is the replenishment and production pool.
  - SEL1 (the D-04 interim reference) holds a secondary cache for receiver-side and tug items.
  - Spares to the NEA ride the lightly loaded tug leg toward the asteroid.
- **Precision parts stay Earth-supplied throughout 0B.** This covers bearings, rad-hard electronics, HV switchgear, battery cells, thrusters and cathodes, seals and solar cells.

- **EP thruster and cathode life on iodine or argon is a top cost driver.** Abrasive wear at the regolith interface is the other. Claude and GPT rank thruster life first. Gemini flags iodine attack on grids as its key open question. All three tie the budget to the D-05 life tests.
- **Robotic exchange in regolith dust, especially through 1–3 kV connectors, is a gating technology.**
  - It must be demonstrated on the 0A pathfinder at TRL 4–5.
  - It must reach TRL 6 in a relevant environment at KDP-0B with no waivers.
  - Demonstrated recovery from failed or jammed swaps is required, not only nominal swaps.
- **Prognostics and health monitoring drives replacement.** This means a digital twin or traveller per serialised unit, plus a deterministic safe state when a swap fails (the mechanism latched or parked, never free). Ground supervises criticality-1 swaps only.
- **Storage must be conditioned and shelf-life qualified.**
  - Electronics are held within about −20 to +40 °C. Claude specifies 0–25 °C, with batteries at partial state of charge.
  - Batteries, lubricants, seals and HV insulation need storage-equivalent qualification of up to about 3 years in deep space.
  - Storage and maintenance loads must be fed into the bom-0-5 power budget.

  - Claude recommends a 10-year basis of P10 $1.1B / P50 $2.0B / P90 $3.4B. This is roughly $600M of initial provisioning plus about $145M/yr. Claude says the round-2 Claude $0.5–1.5B figure is too low because it under-weights thruster wear and robot attrition.

  - GPT suggests $0.65–1.55B over 5 years including robots. GPT treats $0.8–2.5B as a defensible high-risk envelope but not the default.
  - On a common 5-year basis, Claude's P50 is about $1.3–1.4B, inside GPT's range. The real gap is in the time horizon and the treatment of the tail.
- **Imported spares mass:**
  - Claude recommends planning for 150–600 t over 10 years, about 27 t/yr at steady state plus 105–150 t of initial provisioning. That is about 15–30 kg per tonne of product. Claude's drivers are thrusters, wear parts and eclipse-cycled batteries.
  - Gemini prefers 40–60 t as the initial cache.
  - GPT suggests 80–180 t delivered over 5 years, with 45–60% deployed initially.
- **Tug sparing and servicing location:**
  - Claude recommends SEL1 as the mandatory logistics hub. Class-L tug units such as thrusters and array segments would be swapped there by the node manipulator in 24–72 h. Claude would also add a contingency kit of about 2 t at the NEA and require N+k thruster redundancy for ≥99% probability of completing a round trip without service.
  - Gemini prefers routing all spares through SEL1, with tug self-maintenance there left as an open question.
  - GPT suggests using SEL1 only where trajectories justify it. GPT would add small tug-carried recovery kits, installed fault tolerance for in-transit failures, and an explicit whole-tug-loss policy. That policy would choose between fleet margin, a funded replacement tug, or reduced delivery.

## Open Questions

1. **Thruster life.** What are the demonstrated cathode, wall and grid erosion lifetimes of 100 kW-class thrusters on iodine and on argon? Does argon force a different thruster class with different unit sizes?
   - This is the largest single cost lever. In Claude's estimate, a 15 kh life roughly doubles the tug line and a 60 kh life halves it.
2. **Wear and attrition in vacuum and milli-g.** What are the abrasive wear rates per tonne processed for cutters, liners and screens, including beneficiation rejects? What is the annual loss rate of tethered robots? Claude's assumed range is 5–25%/yr, which it calls the least-known number in the item.
3. **Target-specific resupply.** What are the real replenishment opportunities and lead times for the selected NEA? GPT argues these may dominate inventory more than component reliability does.
4. **Tug servicing and whole-tug loss.** Can tugs present propulsion modules for robotic exchange, and where: at SEL1 only, or at the NEA as well? What is the right trade between N+k installed redundancy and loose spares? How should a lost tug be covered?
5. **Site-power eclipse cycling.**
   - Does bom-0-5 avoid eclipse? Claude estimates this alone swings spares mass by up to about 150 t.
   - Which stored spares need conditioning power, and what happens to them after a prolonged power loss?
6. **Local manufacture and retention.** At what import fraction do Fe-Ni wear parts with imported hardfacing break even against launch cost? What retention or disposal requirement will the licensing state impose on failed units under the D-03 ALARP regime?

## Recommended Approach

1. **Size spares by item, from demand physics and lead time; reject the flat 20% buffer.**
   - Adopt a multi-echelon model (Earth, SEL1 cache, NEA forward depot) with random, wear-out and attrition demand classes.
   - Set criticality-based stock-out targets. Claude's α = 2% for production-stopping items is the starting point, to be tightened toward GPT's 0.5–1% where the model shows it is affordable.
   - Couple the model to a tug-traffic simulation.
   - Re-size at KDP-0B to the selected target and to signed Phase 1 demand.
2. **Carry the 0B budget as a rate plus initial provisioning, not a lump sum.**
   - Planning value: about $0.5–0.9B of initial provisioning plus about $70–250M/yr.
   - This gives about $0.65–1.55B over 5 years (P50 about $1.3B) and about $2.0B P50 over 10 years.
   - Place the P50–P90 increment in bom-0-17 as a named, quantified risk.
   - Report a $/kg-of-product metric to the economics gate. Claude estimates about $155/kg at P50.
3. **Include robot attrition and whole-robot replacements in bom-0-14.** bom-0-2 then means the initial fleet only. Require an explicit whole-tug-loss decision at the gate, choosing between bom-0-4 fleet margin, a funded replacement, or a contracted shortfall.
4. **Use SEL1 as the tug-servicing and consolidation point while D-04 holds.**
   - Hold NEA-critical stock at the NEA, sized for the full resupply interval (18 months to 4 years).
   - Require every tug to carry one standard logistics pod toward the NEA without losing product capacity on the return leg.
   - Keep the hub location-agnostic in case D-04 flips.
5. **Fund 0A enabling work of about $20–45M under a single owner.** This covers the interface standard, the sparing model and reliability database, and dust-chamber and pathfinder swap demonstrations.
   - The pathfinder must log at least 20 swaps and about 200 robot-hours of failure data, and must include one HV connector.
   - Dust-tolerant 1–3 kV exchange, surface Class S/M swap and free-space Class L swap must reach TRL 6 at KDP-0B with no waivers. Fund two parallel HV connector designs.
6. **Buy reliability upstream where it returns more than spares do.**
   - Run joint trades with bom-0-2, -4 and -5 before CDR on actuator MTBF, thruster life, N+k redundancy and eclipse-free site power.
   - Hold commonality to about 400 or fewer part numbers, standardising interfaces rather than internal designs to avoid common-cause defects.
   - Use multi-lot procurement.
   - Make a rad-hard EEE lifetime buy at KDP-0B (Claude estimates about $40–80M).
   - Keep the thruster and PPU line warm rather than making a lifetime buy of thrusters.
7. **Keep the debris and contamination discipline from the outset.**
   - Nothing is jettisoned; packaging must not shed.
   - Failed units go to sealed retention pods or return selectively to SEL1, in compliance with bom-0-15.
   - Carry local Fe-Ni wear-part fabrication only as a gated 0B option, decided around year 3 on in-situ wear data and never credited in the baseline.
